notes.title: The argument list and :argdo
notes.kicker: Field notes · one edit, many files
notes.summary: Name a set of files once, then run the same tested change over every one of them.
notes.limitation: Vim Wilds runs a single buffer, so :argdo cannot be practised here. This note tells you the mechanism exists and what makes it safe; the drilling happens in a real terminal.

activities.title: The list Vim already has
activities.body: Open Vim as `vim src/*.js` and it remembers those files as the argument list. `:args` shows it, `:argadd` and `:argdelete` change it. It is a work list you assembled with the shell, and every file in it is a target you have already agreed to.
activities.contrast: A buffer list is whatever you happened to open. An argument list is what you deliberately asked for.

activities.title: The command :argdo runs once per file
activities.instruction: Watch the per-file payload land on one buffer, then read what the driver adds around it.

commandGroups.explanation: Rewrite every match in this one file. Written out in full, `:argdo %s/staging/production/ge | update` puts this same command in front of every file in the list.

feedback.success: Three matches rewritten in one file.
feedback.why: This is the whole payload. `:argdo` contributes no editing of its own — it walks the argument list and runs exactly this against each entry, which is why a payload you have not tested on one file is a payload you are about to run fifty times.
feedback.contrast: The two additions that make it survive the trip are the `e` flag and `| update`, and neither one shows its value on a single file.

activities.title: Why e and update are not optional
activities.body: Without `e`, the first file with no match raises an error and the run stops there — files you never reached stay untouched, and the ones behind you are already changed. Without `| update`, every edit lives in an unwritten buffer, and Vim refuses to leave the file for the next one. `e` keeps the walk going; `update` writes only the buffers that actually changed.
activities.contrast: `update` writes only modified buffers; `write` writes unconditionally and touches the timestamp of every file you looked at.

activities.title: Spot what this run will leave behind
activities.prompt: Forty files are in the argument list. Someone runs `:argdo %s/oldName/newName/ge` and reports that only the first file changed on disk. What explains it?

options.label: No `| update`, so nothing after the first buffer was written
The `g` flag is missing, so only one match per line was replaced
The `%` range is missing, so only the current line was searched

activities.explanation: The substitution itself is correct — `%` scopes it to the whole file, `g` catches every match on a line, and `e` stops a file without matches from aborting the walk. What is missing is the write. Each file was modified in memory and abandoned unwritten as `:argdo` moved on, so the changes exist nowhere on disk. Adding `| update` writes each buffer that actually changed.

notes.title: Buffers and :bufdo
notes.summary: The same walk over a different set — and the difference is what you can name in advance.
notes.limitation: This note has no exercise. Vim Wilds holds one buffer, so a command that iterates buffers has nothing to iterate; what follows is a briefing on when to reach for it.

activities.title: Two lists, two intentions
activities.body: Every file you open gets a buffer, and `:ls` lists them. `:bufdo` runs a command over all of them, exactly as `:argdo` does over the argument list. The mechanics are identical; the sets are not.
activities.contrast: The argument list is a claim about what you meant to change. The buffer list is a record of what you happened to open.

activities.title: Which one to reach for
activities.body: Prefer `:argdo`. A shell glob is reviewable before you commit to it — you can read `src/**/*.ts` and know what it covers. A buffer list accumulates: the file you opened to check something, the help window, the file a plugin loaded for you. `:bufdo` reaches all of it. Reach for it when the set genuinely is "everything I have open", and `:argdo` the rest of the time.
activities.contrast: `:windo` and `:tabdo` are the same idea again, scoped to visible windows and to tabs.

activities.title: Choose the list to walk
activities.prompt: A rename has to reach every `.ts` file under `src`, in a session where you have also opened two log files and a scratch buffer to check something. Which walk applies the change to exactly the intended set?

options.label: `:bufdo` in the session you already have
`:bufdo`, then undo the changes to the log files afterwards

activities.explanation: `:bufdo` would reach the log files and the scratch buffer, because it walks what is open rather than what you meant. Undoing the collateral afterwards is repair work that a correct list avoids: the glob states the intended set in a form you can read before anything runs, and `:argdo` then applies to that and nothing else.

notes.title: Quickfix as a work list
notes.summary: Let a search decide which places need work, then run one command at each of them.
notes.limitation: Quickfix is a list of positions across files, so it cannot exist in a one-buffer app. The demo below shows the single-file shape of the same idea; the cross-file version is described, not practised.

activities.title: A list of places, not of files
activities.body: `:grep`, `:vimgrep` and a compiler's output all populate the quickfix list: file, line, column, message. `:copen` shows it and `:cnext` walks it. Where the argument list is a set of files you named, the quickfix list is a set of positions something else found for you.

activities.title: Find first, then edit what was found
activities.instruction: Watch a predicate pick the lines and a command edit only those, which is the shape :cdo generalises across files.

commandGroups.explanation: The predicate selects the matching lines and the substitution edits only those. `:cdo` is this same split, with the finding done across every file rather than within one.

feedback.success: Only the two matching lines changed.
feedback.why: Finding and editing are separate steps. `:global` finds within one file and quickfix finds across many, but both hand the same thing to the command that follows: a list of places worth touching.
feedback.contrast: `:global` cannot leave the buffer. Quickfix can, which is the only reason to build one.

activities.title: Per entry, or per file
activities.body: `:cdo` runs your command once for every entry in the list, with the cursor already on that line. `:cfdo` runs it once per file that appears in the list. Choose by what your command does: a cursor-relative edit wants `:cdo`, and a whole-file command such as `%s` wants `:cfdo`, or it will run once per match on the same file.
activities.contrast: `:cdo s/old/new/` edits one line at a time. `:cfdo %s/old/new/ge | update` rewrites each file once.

activities.title: Predict how often the command runs
activities.prompt: A search fills the quickfix list with twelve matches spread across three files. Someone runs `:cdo %s/old/new/ge | update`. What actually happens?

options.label: Each of the three files is rewritten several times over — twelve whole-file passes in all
Three passes, one per file, because %s already covers the file
Twelve edits, each confined to the line the entry points at

activities.explanation: `:cdo` runs once per *entry*, and `%s` ignores where the cursor is and rewrites the whole file every time. The result is correct but wasteful — twelve full-file substitutions and twelve writes where three would do. Pairing a whole-file command with `:cfdo`, or a line-scoped `s/old/new/` with `:cdo`, matches the command to the walk.

notes.title: Non-interactive Vim
notes.kicker: Field notes · Vim without a screen
notes.summary: The same commands you type by hand, handed to Vim from a script or a shell prompt.
notes.limitation: Nothing in this note can run in a browser: it is about invoking Vim as a program from a shell. Read it as a briefing on what is possible, and try it in a terminal.

activities.title: Commands from the outside
activities.body: `vim -c 'command' file` opens the file and runs the command. Stack several with `-c`, finish with `-c wq`, and Vim never waits for you. `ex -sc 'command|wq' file` does the same silently, without drawing a screen — the form to use inside a script. `vim -es` reads Ex commands from standard input for longer sequences.
activities.contrast: `-s` here means silent, not the `-s` that replays a keystroke file. Different flag, same letter.

activities.title: When this beats a pipeline
activities.body: Reach for scripted Vim when the transformation is one you already worked out interactively, and when it depends on things Vim knows and a stream editor does not: the file's own syntax, matching brackets, text objects, marks, a recorded macro. `ex -sc 'g/^import/normal! =='` reindents by the rules of the language. The advantage is not speed, it is that you are running the edit you already tested.
activities.contrast: A pipeline reads text as lines. Vim reads it as a buffer with structure, a cursor, and undo.

activities.title: Choose the invocation
activities.prompt: A release script has to apply one substitution to a generated file, on a build machine with no terminal attached, and fail loudly if anything goes wrong. Which invocation fits?

options.label: `vim -c '%s/old/new/ge' file` and let the script move on
`vim -s keys.txt file`, replaying a recorded keystroke file

activities.explanation: `ex -s` expects no terminal and draws no screen, which is what a build machine needs, and the explicit `wq` writes and exits with a status the script can check. The second leaves Vim open waiting for a human that will never arrive. The third is legitimate for replaying keystrokes but is far more fragile here: a keystroke file depends on cursor position and mode at every step, where one Ex command does not.

notes.title: When to leave Vim
notes.summary: The tool that fits is sometimes not this one, and knowing that is part of the skill.
notes.limitation: This note argues rather than teaches a command, and there is nothing here to practise. It is the counterpart to the tool-choice questions in the curriculum, extended past the edge of Vim.

activities.title: What the other tools are better at
activities.body: `sed` streams: it is the right answer for one regular substitution across files you never need to open. `awk` handles records and fields, so columnar data belongs to it. `jq` understands JSON as a structure, and no regular expression over JSON is ever really correct. A written script gets version control, tests and a name.
activities.contrast: Vim's advantage is that the buffer has structure and a cursor. Where the input has no structure Vim understands, that advantage is gone.

activities.title: The question worth asking
activities.body: Ask whether the change has to be re-run. A one-off correction across files you are already reading is Vim's; it needs no artefact and you can see every result. A transformation that will run again, on input you have not seen, in a pipeline someone else maintains, wants a script — something reviewable, testable and re-runnable. Keystroke count is the wrong axis. Blast radius, repeatability and who reads it next are the right ones.
activities.grammar: one-off and visible → Vim · repeated and unattended → a script

activities.title: Decide where this work belongs
activities.prompt: A nightly job must rewrite one field in a large JSON export, every night, on files nobody opens. What should own the transformation?

options.label: A checked-in `jq` program the job invokes
`ex -sc` with a substitution, called from the job

activities.explanation: This is repeated, unattended work on structured input nobody reviews, which is every argument against doing it in an editor. `jq` parses the JSON rather than pattern-matching its text, so it cannot be defeated by reordered keys, escaping or whitespace, and a checked-in program can be reviewed and tested. Both Vim answers would work on the files you tested and would fail silently on the first export shaped differently.
